claims.text: A thin refractory-metal interfacial coating such as Mo will reduce thermal contact resistance at W–Cu interfaces.
The coating will enhance phonon transmission across the W–Cu interface.
Reducing interfacial thermal resistance will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
The refractory-metal coating will preserve mechanical durability.
The refractory-metal coating will preserve irradiation resistance.
Physical-vapor deposition onto W particles or the interface, followed by controlled sintering, can integrate a thin Mo layer into a W–Cu composite.
The refractory-metal coating will form a graded interfacial zone.
The graded interfacial zone will bridge lattice mismatch between tungsten and copper.
The graded interfacial zone will reduce interfacial defects and scattering sites.
Minimizing lattice discontinuities will lower interfacial thermal-barrier resistance.
The inherent properties of the refractory metal will maintain mechanical integrity.
The inherent properties of the refractory metal will resist irradiation-induced damage.
The coated W–Cu composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The coated composite will show no significant loss of mechanical strength relative to the uncoated control.
The coated composite will show no significant loss of irradiation resistance relative to the uncoated control.
Standard uncoated W–Cu composites have higher interfacial thermal resistance.
The improvement should persist under reactor-relevant temperatures and irradiation conditions.
Helium implantation is a relevant irradiation test for fusion-reactor materials.
Excessive coating thickness or poor adhesion could create stress concentrations and undermine mechanical durability.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase, or observation of reduced durability or irradiation resistance, would falsify the hypothesis.
